The starters scaffolded a talker for `board = "qemu-armv7a-nuttx"` (QEMU's
Arm `virt` machine) or `board = "rv-virt-nuttx"` (QEMU's RISC-V `rv-virt`),
linked it into a bootable NuttX kernel with `nros build`, and heard it from
ROS 2. This page covers what comes after them: the image's configuration,
what is particular to each board, adding nano-ros to a NuttX tree you build
with NuttX's own `make`, and the native build.

## Configure the platform

Your application's deployment (board, RMW, domain and an optional
`locator`) is the bringup's `system.toml`, compiled into the image. With a
`locator` added, the image reads:

```toml
[image.nuttx]
board = "qemu-armv7a-nuttx"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:8200"
```

The file is the same whatever language the node is written in, and nothing
in it names a target triple: `armv7a-nuttx-eabihf` is a fact about the
board, and the board's descriptor states it. The guest's network comes from
the board as well: `eth0` at `10.0.2.15`, with QEMU's gateway `10.0.2.2`.
With no `locator`, as scaffolded, the image dials `tcp/10.0.2.2:7447`. Start
the router as the starter did, listening on the host's `0.0.0.0` at the port
the image dials (8200 here); the guest cannot reach a router on `127.0.0.1`.

An image for the other board sits beside the first in the same bringup:

```toml
[image.nuttx_rv]
board = "rv-virt-nuttx"
```

With two images, name the one you run: `nros run nuttx` or
`nros run nuttx_rv`.

## Board notes

- **`qemu-armv7a-nuttx`: QEMU's Arm `virt`,** with a virtio-net device on
  QEMU's user-mode network. `nros run` boots the kernel with the store's
  `qemu-system-arm` and `-icount shift=auto`.
- **`rv-virt-nuttx`: QEMU's RISC-V `virt`, a 32-bit `rv32imac` core.** The
  store's QEMU is built for Arm and RISC-V 64 only, so this board needs a
  `qemu-system-riscv32` from your distribution (Debian and Ubuntu:
  `qemu-system-misc`), named with `QEMU_SYSTEM_RISCV32`. A Rust node builds
  for the board's `riscv32imac-unknown-nuttx-elf` target with `build-std`.
- **C is the runtime-checked language;** read the board's support page for
  what its Rust and C++ rows show.
- **A Rust node needs a configured kernel.** For one, `nros build` first
  configures and exports the NuttX kernel from the board's config (a current
  export is a no-op), then builds the entry with the board's pinned nightly
  toolchain. The configure is NuttX's own `tools/configure.sh`, which needs
  the kconfig-frontends tools; `nros setup <board> --sudo` installs them.
- **The console is the NSH console.** A `nros build` image runs your node at
  boot. The readiness signal is the first `Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'`,
  within about six seconds of boot.
- **No NuttX hardware board ships.** On real hardware the image is an
  ordinary NuttX application, built with that board's `BOARD_CONFIG` and
  flashed as NuttX's documentation for the board says; see
  [Flash a real board](flash-a-real-board.md).

## Add nano-ros to a NuttX tree you build with make

When your NuttX board ships its own kernel build, nano-ros joins it as an
external application under `apps/external/nano-ros/`, with its Kconfig
options under *Application Configuration › External Modules › nano-ros*.
This road needs a NuttX 12 or later checkout of your own, with an `apps/`
tree beside it (`$NUTTX_DIR`, `$NUTTX_APPS_DIR`). In that tree, NuttX owns the
build verb, `make`, the way Zephyr owns `west build`:

1. Provision the board, then stage the integration shell into your apps
   tree once: `"$(nros locate nano-ros)/scripts/nuttx/stage-external-apps.sh" "$NUTTX_APPS_DIR"`.
   It writes `external/Make.defs` and `Kconfig`, and links the shell in as
   `external/nano-ros`. Remove `$NUTTX_APPS_DIR/Kconfig` so NuttX rediscovers
   `apps/external/Kconfig`.
2. Bring the symbols nano-ros needs into your configuration. Stock
   `qemu-armv7a/nsh` has no `CONFIG_NET`, no virtio-net and no `TLS_NELEM`.
   With no configuration of your own, configure from the board's config,
   `packages/boards/nros-board-nuttx-qemu/nuttx-config/arm/defconfig`. It
   `#include`s upstream's `qemu-armv7a:nsh` and lists only what differs, so
   NuttX's own `tools/configure.sh` must expand it; copying it to `.config`
   does not work. Put it in a directory beside a link to
   `boards/arm/qemu/qemu-armv7a/scripts/Make.defs`, and pass that directory to
   `tools/configure.sh -a <apps dir, relative to the kernel>`. configure.sh
   runs `kconfig-tweak`, so it needs the kconfig-frontends tools (Debian and
   Ubuntu: `kconfig-frontends-nox`). With a vendor defconfig, merge the requirements into
   it instead: `CONFIG_NET=y`, `CONFIG_NET_TCP=y`, `CONFIG_NET_IPv4=y`, the
   virtio-net options, `CONFIG_TLS_NELEM=8`, `CONFIG_LIBCXXTOOLCHAIN=y` and
   `CONFIG_ALLSYMS=n`. Then run `make olddefconfig`.
3. Enable nano-ros in `make menuconfig`, or with `kconfig-tweak` from the
   `kconfig-frontends` package: `NROS`, the API you use (`NROS_C_API`,
   `NROS_CPP_API`), and the RMW. These options decide what the shell
   compiles into `libnros_c.a`; they must name the same RMW as your
   `system.toml`.
4. Prepare the workspace, so the generated message bindings exist before
   anything compiles against them: `nros configure`, in the workspace.
5. Build the kernel with `make` in `$NUTTX_DIR`. The Rust static libraries
   build as a sub-step of the app build, and the kernel ELF is
   `$NUTTX_DIR/nuttx`.

A kernel built this way boots to the NSH prompt. Run your app by its
program name there, for example `nsh> nuttx_c_talker`: the build registers
each app as an NSH built-in command. Several apps each declare their own
program name and share the one `libnros_c.a`.

The staging script stages the shell only. A bringup with several components
is built with `nros build` and an `[image.<id>]`, as in
[`examples/workspaces/rust`](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/examples/workspaces/rust/src/demo_bringup/system.toml).

## Read the run plan

From the starter's workspace, print the plan `nros run` follows:

```bash probe=410
nros run nx_node --dry-run --why
```

The plan names the QEMU runner and the board's machine, the console, and the
link to the router at the image's `locator`. `--why` names where each fact
came from.

## Drive the native build yourself

Print the exact commands `nros build` runs, and the QEMU line that boots the
kernel, without building:

```bash probe=420
nros build --dry-run
```

The same QEMU line boots a kernel you built with `make`. `nros configure`
writes the generated entry without building.

## If it doesn't work

If no `Publishing:` line appears:

1. Confirm the app ran: `ps` at the NSH prompt shows its task.
2. Confirm the network: `ifconfig` shows `eth0` at `10.0.2.15`.
3. Confirm the router listens on the host's `0.0.0.0` at the port the
   image's `locator` names.
4. On RISC-V, confirm `QEMU_SYSTEM_RISCV32` names a `qemu-system-riscv32`.

For DDS on NuttX, raise the network buffer options in the kernel
configuration. Everything else: [Troubleshoot](../deploy/troubleshoot.md).
